table.text: The study protocol was reviewed by the Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital/Moi University Institutional Scientific and Ethics Review Committee (Approval number FAN:0005076).

Between 10 July -28 October 2025, 707 SMC-eligible children aged 3-59 months were enrolled. 181 participants who were reported positive by microscopy had a negative PCR result and were subsequently excluded from data analysis.
An additional 17.3% were enrolled 26-31 days post-SMC, during the period when they were awaiting the next cycle.
About 12% of participants were enrolled within 7 days of their last reported SMC dose.

Overall, 14.8% of children were enrolled 26-31 days post-SMC, potentially a window of waning protection as they awaited the next cycle or identified as febrile at home and referred to the facility by the drug distributor.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) is an important malaria prevention strategy used widely in areas of West Africa with highly seasonal transmission.
Monthly administration of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine (SPAQ) to young children during the hightransmission season substantially reduces malaria morbidity and mortality.
SMC has recently been introduced in northern Kenya, where pastoralist communities experience intense malaria transmission.

However, implementation in this setting presents unique challenges, including population mobility, vast distances, dispersed settlements, and high levels of parasite resistance to SP in parts of the region.
Effective surveillance is needed to identify gaps in SMC delivery and uptake and to monitor threats to program effectiveness.

We implemented an innovative sentinel-site surveillance approach in which every malaria case among SMC-eligible children at selected health facilities was investigated to identify gaps in SMC delivery, uptake, and effectiveness.
We also assessed the prevalence of parasite alleles associated with SP and AQ resistance and examined their relationship with SMC uptake.
Household travel was substantially more common than caregiver refusal among reported reasons for missing an SMC cycle.
More than one-third of children presenting with malaria had missed their most recent SMC cycle, while 15% were within a few days of receiving the next scheduled cycle.

The prevalence of SP resistance mutations was considerably lower than reported in other parts of East Africa: only 13.4% of infections carried the quintuple mutant haplotype IRNI/GEAA (PfDHFR 51I, 59R, 108N, PfDHPS 437G, 540E) associated with high level resistance to SP.
However, the prevalence of resistance-associated mutations was higher among children who had recently received SMC.
The allele associated with reduced susceptibility to AQ was not detected.

text.text: Ultimately, malaria risk was reduced by over two thirds.
Robust surveillance systems are lacking in high or moderate malaria transmission regions of Sub-Saharan Africa, which bear the greatest burden of malaria.
This study focused on children presenting with a positive malaria diagnosis during the 2025 transmission season to identify underlying reasons for suboptimal protection during SMC.
The overall goal was to use surveillance to investigate reasons for illness and improve the SMC program in real time.
Turkana County is the largest county in Kenya but is sparsely populated and predominantly rural.
Turkana residents are primarily nomadic pastoralists whose movement is shaped by the arid environment and the seasonal rainfall.
Despite the arid climate and low population density, malaria transmission is very high, exceeding 400 cases per 1000 people in an average season.
In 2024, Turkana County piloted SMC in one subcounty to protect young children from malaria infection.
After the success of the first campaign, Turkana County implemented its second round of SMC from June-October 2025.
As in the previous round, sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine and Amodiaquine (SPAQ) was delivered over a five-day interval to all children between 3-59 months in Turkana Central subcounty.
The first cycle was initiated on 05/06/2025 and repeated every 28 days for five total cycles.
Sentinel surveillance was initiated on 10/07/2025, immediately following the second cycle of SMC.
Enrollment ended on 28/10/2025, 28 days after the final day of the final cycle of SMC.

text.text: A sentinel event was defined as an SMC-eligible child aged 3-59 months who lived in the SMC implementing sub county (Turkana Central) between July-October 2025 and had a positive malaria diagnosis by malaria rapid diagnostic test (mRDT) or microscopy at one of the participating facilities.
Children presenting to the facility who were referred for a malaria diagnostic test were screened for eligibility.
The accompanying parent or guardian was invited to participate in the study if the child met the criteria for enrollment.
A trained nurse or clinical officer sought written informed consent from the parent or guardian.
A standardized questionnaire was administered in KOBOCollect to capture basic information including age, geographical residence, bed net use, history of malaria-like illness, and SMC information.
SMC questions explored whether SMC cycles were missed and why, the date of the last SMC drugs, adherence to the 3-day regimen, adverse reactions and vomiting during drug administration.
Data were entered directly into tablets and synced to an encrypted passwordprotected server.
For children older than 6 months, a Dried Blood Spot (DBS) was prepared by dropping 5-10 µL of blood on to a filter paper and allowing it to dry completely.
Children under 6 months of age were exempted from DBS sample collection, but their caregivers participated in the questionnaire.
The study protocol was reviewed by the Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital/Moi University Institutional Scientific and Ethics Review Committee (Approval number FAN:0005076).

An additional 17.3% were enrolled 26-31 days post-SMC, during the period when they were awaiting the next cycle.
It is possible that many of these were referred to the health facility by the drug distributor if they were found unwell during the campaign.
About 12% of participants were enrolled within 7 days of their last reported SMC dose.

Some of these children may have had a non-malaria illness (or even SPAQ side effects) but also harbored an asymptomatic infection that was still detectable by mRDT when they reported to the health facility.

text.text: When community-based testing is unavailable, as in Turkana, all children who are unwell are referred to the facility and not given SMC at home.
Often those referrals are not completed and consequently that child will not receive SMC.
The finding that nearly a quarter of missed SMC cycles was due to illness at the time of distribution suggests two priority areas for improving SMC coverage in subsequent campaigns.
First, aligning the first cycle of SMC to begin before significant seasonal transmission could reduce the number of children who were already infected and therefore ineligible for SMC.
Second, strengthening community-based malaria testing could facilitate delivery of SMC to malaria-negative children experiencing symptoms on the day of distribution.

text.text: This study investigated children who presented to health facilities with malaria in six sentinel facilities.
We purposively selected facilities which serve different types of populations (pastoralist, peri-urban, fishing communities) and represent varying malaria burden.
As a result, the findings may not be generalizable but rather indicative.
We relied heavily on the caregiver report of uptake of SMC which may not be completely accurate, probably erring on the side of higher uptake and adherence.

The finding that microscopy results included a large numbers of false positives is problematic generally, but specifically for SMC may lead to declining confidence in the efficacy of the treatment if children take SMC but are subsequently being diagnosed with and treated for malaria.

Our results suggest that SMC with SPAQ is expected to be highly effective in this setting.
Measures should be taken to preserve the useful lifespan of SPAQ and safeguard against increasing resistance by reinforcing the importance of adhering to the complete monthly regimen.
Sentinel site monitoring through case investigation at health facilities can generate actionable information in real-time to assist SMC programming.
